sample.note: Sample data. Fictional company and people. Replace before use.

documents.title: Business Case
documents.summary: Why the project is worth doing: options, costs, benefits, NPV and the decision you need.

when.create: Before funding approval, after the idea is shaped enough to cost (typically 2-4 weeks before the investment committee).
when.update: At each stage gate, and whenever cost or benefits move by more than 10%.

how: Start from the decision you need and work backwards
Show at least three options, including do nothing
Get Finance to validate the cost model and discount rate
Run a sensitivity check: what if benefits are 40% lower?
Keep the main body to 6-8 pages; put workings in an appendix

who.author: Project / Program Manager
who.contributors: Finance, Product, Tech Lead, benefit owners

documents.mistake: Writing it to justify a decision already made. If no option could ever lose, reviewers stop trusting it.
documents.plain: The argument for spending the money: what it costs, what we get back, and why this option beats the others.
documents.like: Like comparing quotes before a home renovation and working out whether it adds enough value to the house.
documents.without: Money gets spent on projects nobody can later prove were worth it.

documents.title: Project Charter
documents.summary: Formally authorises the project and the PM: objectives, scope, milestones, budget, governance.

when.create: Immediately after the business case is approved, before the team mobilises.
when.update: Only through approved change requests that alter objectives, scope boundaries, budget envelope or governance.

how: Keep it to 3-5 pages
Lift objectives and budget from the approved business case
Write scope as lists of deliverables, not activities
Set explicit tolerances (cost, time) and who can approve changes
Walk the sponsor through it in person before asking for a signature
documents.mistake: Treating it as paperwork. A charter without tolerances means every slip becomes a negotiation.
documents.plain: The official 'go ahead' for the project. It says what we will deliver, by when, for how much, and who is in charge.
documents.like: Like the signed agreement with a builder before work starts.
documents.without: People disagree later about what was promised, and the project manager has no authority to make calls.

documents.title: Stakeholder Register
documents.summary: Everyone affected by the project, how much they matter, and the engagement plan for each.
inside: Interest and influence scores with calculated quadrant
Attitude and current vs desired engagement

when.create: Week 1, before kickoff invitations go out.
when.update: Monthly, plus after re-organisations, new phases or a stakeholder changes role.

how: Brainstorm with the sponsor: who gains, who loses, who can block
Score interest and influence 1-5; the quadrant calculates
Write their actual concern in their words
Plan actions for every row where current engagement is below desired
Keep it private: it holds candid judgements
what: Key concerns raised since last review
documents.mistake: Listing names and never scoring attitude. The value is in spotting the gap between current and desired engagement.
documents.plain: A list of everyone the project affects or who can affect it, how much they care, and how we'll keep them on side.
documents.like: Like a wedding planner's guest list with notes on who needs special attention.
documents.without: Someone important gets surprised late and blocks or delays the work.

documents.title: RACI Matrix
documents.summary: Who is Responsible, Accountable, Consulted and Informed for each key activity.
inside: Automatic check: exactly one A per row

when.create: During mobilisation, before the first sprint or work package starts.
when.update: When roles change, a vendor joins, or a decision gets stuck because nobody owns it.

how: List decisions and deliverables, not daily tasks
Exactly one Accountable per row (the check column flags errors)
Limit C's: every C is a meeting or a review cycle
Review it live with all named roles so they agree, not just see it
what: Rows where reality differs from the plan
documents.mistake: Two A's on one row. Shared accountability means nobody is accountable.
documents.plain: A grid that shows, for each task, who does it, who signs it off, who gets asked, and who just gets told.
documents.like: Like a household chore chart that also says who checks the job was done.
documents.without: Work falls between the cracks, or two people both think they're in charge.

documents.title: Project Management Plan
documents.summary: How the project will be run: approach, scope, schedule, cost, quality, risk, resources, comms and vendors.
inside: Delivery approach and definition of done
Scope, schedule and cost control with tolerances

when.create: During planning; baselined at the design / planning gate.
when.update: When the approach changes (e.g. moving to agile build) or after a re-baseline.

how: Describe how you will manage, not the work itself
Link to the detailed logs instead of copying their content
State numeric thresholds: what triggers escalation
Scale it: 5 pages for a small project, 20 for a regulated one

who.author: Project Manager
who.contributors: Delivery Manager, Tech Lead, QA Lead, Finance

documents.mistake: A 60-page plan no one reads. If it does not change behaviour, cut it.
documents.plain: The rulebook for running the project: how we'll track time, money, quality and risk, and when we escalate.
documents.like: Like the house rules a team agrees before a long trip: who drives, who books, what happens if we're late.
documents.without: Everyone runs things their own way and problems get escalated too late, or not at all.

documents.title: Project Schedule (Gantt)
documents.summary: Integrated WBS schedule with a self-drawing weekly Gantt, status-date line and milestone tracker.
inside: WBS with owners, dates, % complete and predecessors
Gantt bars that redraw from dates
Milestone tab with baseline vs forecast variance

when.create: During planning, once scope and the delivery approach are agreed.
when.update: Weekly: % complete and forecast dates. Baseline only through change control.

how: Build top-down from deliverables (WBS), then sequence
Keep tasks between 1 and 4 weeks for tracking
Get estimates from the people doing the work
Mark the critical path and milestones
Update forecast dates honestly; never overwrite the baseline
documents.mistake: Updating the baseline every week so variance is always zero. Then you can't see slippage.
documents.plain: The timeline: every piece of work with start and end dates, drawn as bars so you can see what overlaps and what is late.
documents.like: Like a wedding-day timeline, but stretched over months.
documents.without: Nobody can see that a delay in one task will push back everything after it.

documents.title: Budget and EVM Tracker
documents.summary: Monthly planned value, earned value and actual cost with CPI, SPI, EAC, TCPI and an S-curve.
inside: Monthly and cumulative PV / EV / AC
SV, CV, SPI, CPI with RAG
Budget vs forecast by cost category

when.create: At baseline, once the schedule and cost estimate are agreed.
when.update: Monthly, after finance close (working day 3-5). Forecast monthly; actuals from the ledger.

how: Spread budget over time to get PV
Earn value only for measurable progress (0/50/100 rule for small tasks)
Take actuals from finance, not timesheets alone
Explain every variance over 5% in one line
Forecast at completion with judgement, not just the formula
documents.mistake: Using % spent as % complete. EV must come from delivered work, otherwise CPI is always 1.0.
documents.plain: Tracks money: what we planned to spend by now, what we actually spent, and how much work that money really got done.
documents.like: Like checking a renovation: half the budget is gone, but is half the house finished?
documents.without: Overspending is noticed only when the money runs out.

documents.title: Resource and Capacity Plan
documents.summary: FTE demand by role and month against capacity, with labour cost and over-allocation flags.
inside: Capacity tab with automatic red flags where demand > capacity

when.create: During planning, alongside the schedule and budget.
when.update: Monthly, and when a role is added, a person leaves, or the schedule moves.

how: Plan by role first, then name people
Get capacity from line managers net of leave and BAU work
Resolve every red cell: hire, re-sequence, or descope
Reconcile labour cost with the budget tracker
documents.mistake: Planning people at 100%. Real productive capacity is 70-80% after meetings and support.
documents.plain: Shows how many people of each kind we need each month, compared with how many we actually have.
documents.like: Like a restaurant rota: are there enough chefs on Saturday night?
documents.without: Some people are overloaded and burn out while work waits for skills nobody booked.

documents.title: Communication Plan
documents.summary: What is communicated, to whom, why, how often, in what format and by whom.
inside: 8 standard communications from stand-up to SteerCo
Audience, purpose, format, frequency, owner, channel

when.create: During planning, right after the stakeholder register.
when.update: At each phase change and when stakeholders say they are over- or under-informed.

how: Derive audiences from the stakeholder register
Every 'manage closely' stakeholder must appear at least once
Name a single owner for each communication
Prefer fewer, regular communications over ad hoc emails
documents.mistake: A plan full of broadcasts. Include two-way forums where stakeholders can push back.
documents.plain: Who gets told what, how often and how: weekly emails, monthly meetings, team huddles.
documents.like: Like a school's calendar of parent newsletters and meetings.
documents.without: Some people feel ignored, others are flooded with updates, and rumours fill the gap.

documents.title: Benefits Register
documents.summary: Benefits from the business case with baseline, target, latest actual, owner and measurement date.
inside: % of target calculated (works for up or down measures)

when.create: With the business case; refined during planning.
when.update: At each gate, then at post-go-live review points (e.g. 30, 90, 180 days).

how: Measure the baseline before work starts
Assign each benefit to a business owner, not the PM
Separate enabling benefits (e.g. single customer view) from financial ones
Agree the data source for each measure now
what: Target dates if the business changes
documents.mistake: No baseline. Without a 'before' number, no 'after' number proves anything.
documents.plain: The list of good things the project promised (faster service, more sales) with how we'll measure them and who checks.
documents.like: Like noting your electricity bill before installing solar panels, so you can prove the saving afterwards.
documents.without: The project finishes but nobody can show it delivered what it promised.

documents.title: RAID Log
documents.summary: Risks, Assumptions, Issues, Dependencies and Decisions in one workbook with heat map and summary.
inside: Risks with 5x5 scoring and automatic heat map

when.create: At kickoff. Seed it from the charter's risks and assumptions.
when.update: Weekly review with workstream leads; add items the day they are found.

how: Write risks as cause, event and effect
Score probability and impact 1-5; escalate at the thresholds
Every item gets an owner and a next action date
Close risks that can no longer happen
Log decisions the day they are made

who.author: Project Manager
who.approver: None; escalations go to Program Manager / SteerCo

documents.mistake: A risk log that only grows. If nothing closes, it's not being managed.
documents.plain: One place to track what might go wrong (Risks), what we're taking for granted (Assumptions), what is going wrong (Issues), what we're waiting on (Dependencies), and what we decided (Decisions).
documents.like: Like a ship captain's log of hazards ahead, problems on board and decisions made.
documents.without: Known problems are forgotten until they explode, and old decisions get argued again.

documents.title: Change Log
documents.summary: Every change request with cost and schedule impact, status and running revised budget.
inside: CR register with type, impact and status
Net approved impact and pending totals

when.create: At baseline.
when.update: Whenever a CR is raised or decided.

how: Log every request, including rejected ones
Link each row to its CR form
Feed approved impacts into the schedule and budget
documents.mistake: Absorbing small changes without logging them. Twenty small changes become a large overrun nobody approved.
documents.plain: A running list of every request to change the plan and whether it was approved, with the extra cost and time.
documents.like: Like the list of extras added to a building contract: 'add a window: +$800, +2 days'.
documents.without: Lots of small extras add up to a big overrun nobody agreed to.

documents.title: Change Request Form
documents.summary: One change, fully assessed: reason, impact on scope/time/cost/quality, options, funding and decision.
inside: Impact on scope, schedule, cost, quality, benefits, other projects

when.create: When a change exceeds the PM's tolerance (e.g. cost > $10k or schedule > 5 days).
when.update: Until decided; then frozen.

how: Quantify all four constraints even when zero
Always show alternatives you rejected
Say where the money comes from
Get impact estimates from the people who will do the work

who.author: Project Manager
who.approver: Per change authority: PM / Program Manager / SteerCo

documents.mistake: Presenting a single option. Approvers need a real choice, or they will ask for one and delay.
documents.plain: The form used to ask for one change to the plan. It explains why, what it will cost, and what the alternatives are, so someone can decide.
documents.like: Like asking your builder for a quote before agreeing to move a wall.
documents.without: Changes slip in through hallway conversations and nobody owns the consequences.

documents.title: Weekly Status Report
documents.summary: One-page weekly status: RAG by dimension, summary, metrics, milestones, top risks and asks.
inside: RAG for overall, schedule, cost, scope, quality, resources

when.create: From week 1.
when.update: Every week, same day (e.g. Friday noon).

how: Write the summary last, for someone who reads nothing else
RAG against tolerances, not gut feel
Every Amber/Red has a recovery action and owner
End with specific asks and dates
Pull numbers from the trackers; don't retype
documents.mistake: Watermelon reporting: green outside, red inside. Report Amber early; Red surprises cost trust.
documents.plain: A one-page weekly update: are we on track (green, amber or red), what got done, what's next, and what help we need.
documents.like: Like a weekly school report for the project.
documents.without: Leaders find out about problems from rumours, or too late to help.

documents.title: Steering Committee Deck
documents.summary: 7-slide SteerCo pack: executive summary, milestones, EVM chart, risks, decision with options, asks.

when.create: Before the first SteerCo.
when.update: Monthly (or per SteerCo), sent 2 working days before.

how: Title each slide with the message, not the topic
Put the decision on slide 2
Pre-wire: brief each member 1:1 before the meeting
Keep detail in the appendix
documents.mistake: Using SteerCo to report status. Its job is decisions; status can be read beforehand.
documents.plain: Slides for the monthly meeting with senior leaders who make the big decisions about the project.
documents.like: Like a board meeting pack: short, focused on the decisions needed.
documents.without: Big decisions get delayed because leaders don't have what they need to decide.

documents.title: Steering Committee Minutes
documents.summary: Decision-focused minutes: attendees, summary, decisions with IDs, actions with owners and dates.

when.create: Within 24 hours of each SteerCo.
when.update: Action status at the next meeting.

how: Record decisions and actions, not a transcript
One owner and one date per action
Copy decisions into the RAID decision log
Get the chair to confirm before wide circulation
documents.mistake: Actions owned by 'the team'. Without a named owner nothing happens.
documents.plain: The written record of what senior leaders decided in their meeting and who will do what by when.
documents.like: Like the minutes of a residents' association meeting.
documents.without: People remember decisions differently and agreed actions never happen.

documents.title: Project Health Dashboard
documents.summary: One-screen view: KPI tiles (SPI, CPI, % complete, EAC, days to go-live), RAG by dimension, charts.
inside: KPI tiles calculated from a Data tab

when.create: Once baseline and trackers exist.
when.update: Weekly (RAG) and monthly (financials).

how: Feed it from the trackers, never type numbers twice
Limit to what drives decisions: 6 KPIs, 3 charts
Show trend, not just a snapshot
documents.mistake: A dashboard with 30 metrics. If everything is shown, nothing stands out.
documents.plain: A single page of the most important numbers and colours that show at a glance how healthy the project is.
documents.like: Like a car dashboard: speed, fuel and warning lights in one view.
documents.without: People have to dig through many files to know if something is wrong.

documents.title: Agile Sprint Metrics
documents.summary: Velocity, say/do ratio, scope added, rolling average forecast and a daily sprint burndown.
inside: Sprint table with say/do % and 3-sprint rolling average

when.create: At sprint 1.
when.update: Daily (burndown) and at each sprint review (velocity).

how: Use the rolling average, not the best sprint, to forecast
Track scope added mid-sprint separately
Never compare velocity across teams
documents.mistake: Turning velocity into a target. Teams will inflate estimates and the forecast breaks.
documents.plain: Tracks how much work the team finishes in each two-week cycle (a 'sprint'), so we can predict when the rest will be done.
documents.like: Like tracking how many kilometres you run each week to predict when you'll be ready for a marathon.
documents.without: Delivery dates are guesses, and teams take on more than they can finish.

documents.title: Quality and Delivery Metrics
documents.summary: DORA measures, test coverage, pass rate, escaped defects with sparklines, plus defect trend by severity.
inside: 8 KPIs with target, 4-month trend, direction and auto RAG
Defects found by severity vs closed, with backlog

when.create: When build starts.
when.update: Monthly (KPIs); weekly during test phases (defects).

how: Automate data pulls from CI/CD and test tools where possible
Look at 3-month trends before acting
Agree targets with the tech lead, not top-down
documents.mistake: Celebrating a high test pass rate when coverage is low. Measure both.
documents.plain: Measures how good and how reliable the software work is: how often it's released, how often releases break, how many bugs are found.
documents.like: Like a factory tracking defects per batch and how quickly the line restarts after a stoppage.
documents.without: Quality problems surface only when customers find them.

documents.title: Program / Portfolio Dashboard
documents.summary: All projects in one view: RAG by dimension, budget vs actual, SPI/CPI, next milestone, high risks.
inside: Row per project with RAG, financials and indices
RAG doughnut and budget vs actual chart

when.create: When the program or PMO is set up.
when.update: Weekly (each PM updates their row by a fixed time).

how: Use the same RAG definitions on every project
Make PMs own their rows; PMO checks consistency
Red projects need a recovery plan within 5 working days
documents.mistake: Different RAG rules per project, so the portfolio view compares apples with oranges.
documents.plain: One view of several related projects together, so leaders can see which need attention.
documents.like: Like an air-traffic control screen showing every plane at once.
documents.without: Leaders can't compare projects or spot a struggling one in time.

documents.title: UAT Sign-off Certificate
documents.summary: Formal business acceptance: test results by area, open defects with workarounds, criteria and conditions.
inside: Open defects with workaround and fix date

when.create: Before UAT starts (criteria); completed at UAT exit.
when.update: Frozen after sign-off.

how: Agree acceptance criteria before testing begins
List every open defect with a workaround
Make conditions explicit and dated
Signatories are business owners, not the project team
documents.mistake: Asking for sign-off on criteria nobody agreed in advance. Then sign-off becomes a negotiation.
documents.plain: The business's formal 'yes, this works for us' after real users have tested the new system.
documents.like: Like the final walk-through of a new house before you accept the keys.
documents.without: A system goes live that the people using it never agreed was ready.

documents.title: Go/No-Go Checklist
documents.summary: Readiness criteria across product, operations, people and data, with owners and the final decision.
inside: Criteria grouped by product, operations, people, data
Ready? Yes/No with owner and evidence

when.create: 4-6 weeks before go-live.
when.update: Daily in go-live week; final at the decision meeting.

how: Agree criteria early so the meeting is a check, not a debate
Every criterion needs evidence, not opinion
A 'No' on a mandatory item is a no-go unless the sponsor accepts the risk in writing
documents.mistake: Deciding go-live by momentum. Have the courage to say no-go when criteria are missed.
documents.plain: The final checklist before launch. Each item must be 'yes' before we switch the new system on.
documents.like: Like a pilot's pre-flight checklist.
documents.without: Launch happens because the date arrived, not because everything was ready.

documents.title: Cutover Runbook
documents.summary: Minute-by-minute go-live plan with owners, checks, go/no-go points and a rollback plan.
inside: Sequenced steps with planned time, duration, owner, check
Rollback tab with point of no return

when.create: 6-8 weeks before go-live.
when.update: After each rehearsal; live during cutover.

how: Rehearse at least twice with real data volumes
Define the point of no return
Each step has a verifiable check
Have a single cutover lead calling steps
what: Actual start/end and status during cutover
documents.mistake: No rollback rehearsal. A rollback you have never run is a hope, not a plan.
documents.plain: The step-by-step script for launch weekend: who does what, at what time, how we check it worked, and how to undo it if needed.
documents.like: Like a stage manager's cue sheet for opening night.
documents.without: Launch night becomes improvised, and nobody knows how to roll back if it fails.

documents.title: Lessons Learned Report
documents.summary: What went well and what to improve, with impact, concrete recommendations and owners to embed them.

when.create: Start at kickoff; collect at each retrospective and gate.
when.update: Consolidated at closure.

how: Collect throughout, not just at the end
Use a blameless format
Each lesson needs a recommendation and an owner
Send it to the PMO, not a shared drive nobody opens
documents.mistake: 'Communication could be better.' A lesson must be specific enough to change what the next project does.
documents.plain: What went well and what didn't, written down so the next project does better.
documents.like: Like a sports team reviewing match footage.
documents.without: The organisation repeats the same mistakes on every project.

documents.title: Project Closure Report
documents.summary: Final results against baseline, objectives and early benefits, handover, open items and financial closure.
inside: Performance against baseline (time, cost, scope, quality)

when.create: At the end of hypercare / transition.
when.update: Frozen after Gate 4 approval.

how: Compare to the original baseline and to approved changes
Hand every open item to a named owner
Close POs and release unused contingency
Hand benefits tracking to the business
documents.mistake: Closing without handing over benefits tracking. Then nobody ever proves the business case.
documents.plain: The final report: what was delivered compared with what was promised, what's been handed over, and confirmation the project can close.
documents.like: Like the final handover pack when you move out of a rented flat.
documents.without: Loose ends stay open, money stays committed and nobody owns what's left.

documents.title: Skills Matrix
documents.summary: Who can do what, rated 0-4 for every person and skill, with coverage counts that flag single points of failure.
inside: 24 people x 10 skills, rated 0 (none) to 4 (can lead and teach)
People at 3+ and at 4 per skill
Coverage risk per skill: OK, Thin or Gap

when.create: When you set up a resource management function, or take over a team.
when.update: Quarterly, after appraisals, and whenever someone joins, leaves or finishes a certification.

how: Rate with the person and their manager, not alone
Use the 0-4 scale literally: 3 means works without help
Look at the bottom rows first: they show where one resignation leaves you stuck
Feed gaps into hiring and training plans
Never use it as a performance rating

who.author: Resource Manager
who.contributors: Line managers, practice leads, the people themselves

documents.mistake: Rating people from memory. Self-rating plus manager review takes ten minutes and is far more accurate.
documents.plain: A grid of everyone on the team against the skills you sell, showing how good each person is at each one.
documents.like: Like a cricket captain's notes on who can bowl, keep wicket or open the batting.
documents.without: You find out nobody else knows the payment system on the day its only expert resigns.

documents.title: Bench Tracker
documents.summary: Everyone not on billable work, how long they've waited, what it's costing, and the plan to get them deployed.
inside: Bench since, days on bench and bench cost, calculated
Next opportunity and how likely it is
Summary: bench %, average days, 30+ day cases, total cost

when.create: As soon as anyone rolls off a project without a next one.
when.update: Weekly, before the resourcing meeting.

how: Every row needs a next opportunity and an action, even if the action is training
Escalate anyone past 30 days
Use bench time for shadowing, cross-skilling or pre-sales support
Review with account leads, not just HR

who.author: Resource Manager
who.contributors: Account leads, practice leads, talent team

what: Who joined or left the bench
documents.mistake: Treating bench as a holding area. People on the bench for weeks without a plan start looking for other jobs.
documents.plain: A list of people who are between projects, how long they've been waiting, and what's being done to place them.
documents.like: Like the substitutes list in football: who's ready, who needs fitness work, and when they're likely to come on.
documents.without: Good people sit idle for months, cost keeps running, and they quietly leave.

documents.title: Utilisation & Billability Tracker
documents.summary: Weekly hours per person split into billable, non-billable project and internal time, with utilisation and billability against target.
inside: Utilisation and billability per person-week with RAG
Team trend tab with a line chart

when.create: When timesheets are in place and you have targets agreed with finance.
when.update: Weekly, from timesheets (Monday).

how: Agree definitions with finance first: what counts as billable
Subtract leave from available hours
Watch the gap between utilisation and billability: that's work nobody is paying for
Look at 4-week averages before acting on one bad week
documents.mistake: Chasing 100% utilisation. A team with no slack can't absorb a single surprise, and quality pays for it.
documents.plain: Tracks how much of each person's week is spent on work clients pay for, compared with the target.
documents.like: Like a taxi's meter: how many hours the car was out, and how many of those had a paying passenger.
documents.without: The team looks busy, the numbers look fine, and margin quietly leaks through unbilled work.

documents.title: Resource Request Log
documents.summary: Every request for people (the demand pipeline), from first ask to filled or lost, with time to fill and fill rate.
inside: Request ID, account, role, skills, grade, start date, duration
Status: Open, Proposed, Soft booked, Filled, Lost
Time to fill and days until start, calculated
Summary: fill rate, average time to fill, urgent open requests

when.create: The day the first account lead asks for a person.
when.update: Daily or at every resourcing call; weekly review of open requests.

how: Log every request, even the ones you can't fill: lost requests show where to hire
Capture skills and grade, not just a role title
Soft-book early, hard-book when the SOW is signed
Flag anything starting within 3 weeks that is still open
documents.mistake: Taking requests over chat and email. Without one log, two account leads book the same person and nobody notices until Monday.
documents.plain: A queue of every 'I need a person for this project' request, tracked until someone is assigned or the request is dropped.
documents.like: Like a restaurant's booking book: who wants a table, when, for how many, and whether you could seat them.
documents.without: Requests get lost in chats, the same person is promised twice, and new projects start short-staffed.

documents.title: Allocation Heatmap
documents.summary: Each person's planned allocation for the next 12 weeks, coloured to show who is free, healthy or double-booked.
inside: 24 people x 12 weeks of planned allocation %
Colours: under 80% amber, 80-100% blue, over 100% red
Counts of people over 100% and under 50%

when.create: Once requests and bookings are being tracked.
when.update: Weekly, after the resourcing meeting.

how: Include soft bookings, so the pipeline is visible
Resolve every red cell: someone is promised to two places
Use amber weeks to plan training, leave and bench actions
Share it with account leads so they see the trade-offs
documents.mistake: Only tracking this week. Problems are visible six weeks out, when you can still do something about them.
documents.plain: A colour-coded calendar showing how busy each person is planned to be over the next three months.
documents.like: Like a hospital's ward roster: you can see in one glance which shifts are short and who's doing a double.
documents.without: People get double-booked, someone burns out, and a project starts without the person it was promised.

projectCategories.name: Software & Digital Products
projectCategories.plain: Building or changing apps, websites and software products that customers or staff use.

types.name: Agile product build
types.plain: A team builds a new app or product in short two-week cycles, showing working pieces as they go and adjusting based on feedback.
types.examples: New mobile app, customer portal, internal tool

docs.when: Before sprint 0. Keep it light: vision, outcomes, budget envelope, team.
docs.note: Describe outcomes, not a fixed feature list: the backlog holds the detail.
Focus on decision rights between Product Owner, Tech Lead and business.

docs.when: From sprint 1; update daily (burndown) and at every sprint review.
docs.note: This is your primary progress tracker in agile delivery.

docs.when: Review at sprint planning, not in a separate meeting.
Fortnightly, after each sprint review, can replace weekly.
docs.note: Link to the sprint review demo recording.
DORA measures matter most here: release frequency and change failure rate.

docs.when: Monthly. Use cost per sprint as PV if scope is fluid.
docs.note: In agile, earn value per completed story points vs planned points.
Tie benefits to product metrics (activation, retention, conversion).
Backlog reprioritisation is not a change request. Log only changes to budget, date or outcomes.

docs.when: Before each major release, not each sprint.
Feed from every sprint retrospective.

types.name: Website or app redesign
types.plain: Redesigning how an existing website or app looks and works, usually with research, design, then build.
types.examples: Website relaunch, checkout redesign, design system rollout
types.method: Hybrid: research and design phases, agile build

docs.note: Include success metrics from analytics (conversion, task completion) with baselines.
Brand, legal and marketing often have sign-off power: map them early.
Be explicit about who approves designs, otherwise review cycles multiply.
Show research, design, build, content and launch as phases with review rounds.
Use for scope additions after design sign-off.
Include content and accessibility checks, not only function.
Add SEO redirects, analytics tagging and rollback of DNS.

docs.when: Baseline analytics before design starts.

types.name: SaaS / off-the-shelf tool rollout
types.plain: Buying a ready-made software service (like a CRM or HR system), configuring it, moving data in and training people.
types.examples: Salesforce, Workday, ServiceNow, HubSpot rollout

docs.note: Include subscription costs for 3-5 years, not just implementation.
Vendor roadmap changes are a common risk.
Business SMEs for configuration workshops are the bottleneck.
Adoption is the main risk: plan communications to end users.
Include data load and old-system read-only switch.
Track adoption (active users) as an early benefit.

projectCategories.name: Enterprise IT & Systems
projectCategories.plain: Large internal systems that run the business: finance, supply chain, HR, and the connections between systems.

types.name: ERP implementation
types.plain: Replacing the core system a company uses to run finance, orders, stock and purchasing. Big, risky and touches almost every team.
types.examples: SAP S/4HANA, Oracle Fusion, Microsoft Dynamics

docs.note: Formal plan is expected; auditors may review it.
Include every business process owner.

docs.when: Weekly; critical path review fortnightly.
docs.note: Expect 300-1,000 lines. Use the template's structure, scale up.
EVM is expected at this size.
Backfill for business SMEs is a budget item.
One certificate per process area.
Include financial period close and audit readiness.

docs.when: Start 3 months before go-live; at least 3 rehearsals.

types.name: System integration / API platform
types.plain: Connecting systems so they share data automatically, for example making the online shop talk to the stores' tills.
types.examples: Integration layer, API gateway, middleware replacement

docs.note: Each connected system has an owner: list them as roles.
Model each external system's availability as a dependency.
Dependencies tab is critical: every connected system is one.
Track integration test pass rate separately.

types.name: IT service transition / vendor onboarding
types.plain: Moving the running of an IT service from one team or supplier to another without disrupting users.
types.examples: Outsourcing service desk, changing managed-service provider

docs.note: Include the outgoing provider: they may be unmotivated.
Show responsibilities before, during and after handover.
Users must know where to get help on day 1.
Include knowledge transfer completion and service levels.

projectCategories.name: Infrastructure & Cloud
projectCategories.plain: The technical foundations: servers, networks, cloud platforms and security.

types.name: Cloud migration
types.plain: Moving applications and data from the company's own servers to a cloud provider such as AWS, Azure or Google Cloud.
types.examples: Data-centre exit, lift-and-shift, re-platforming

docs.note: Show run-cost comparison over 3-5 years including exit costs.
Plan by migration wave; one row group per wave.
Watch cloud run costs, not just project spend.

docs.when: One runbook per wave.
Per wave.
After every wave, not just at the end.
docs.note: Wave lessons make later waves faster.

types.name: Network or data-centre upgrade
types.plain: Replacing or upgrading physical network equipment or computer rooms, often across many sites.
types.examples: Store network refresh, Wi-Fi rollout, data-centre move

docs.note: Add a rollout tracker tab: one row per site.
Supplier lead times are a frequent risk.
Sites need notice of outage windows.

types.name: Cyber-security remediation
types.plain: Fixing security weaknesses found in an audit or attack, often with a regulator or auditor watching.
types.examples: Audit findings remediation, identity and access overhaul

docs.note: Map each objective to the audit finding it closes.
Treat each finding as an issue with a due date.
Risk committee may replace SteerCo.
Attach evidence of closure for auditors.

projectCategories.name: Data & AI
projectCategories.plain: Projects about moving, organising or using data, from reporting dashboards to machine-learning models.

types.name: Data migration
types.plain: Moving data from an old system to a new one, cleaning and checking it so nothing is lost or wrong.
types.examples: Customer records migration, legacy archive move
types.method: Iterative dry runs, then a final cutover

docs.note: Define 'migrated correctly' as a measurable target (e.g. 99.5% reconciled).
Business data owners must sign off quality, not IT.
Schedule at least two full dry runs.
Data quality is the top risk: profile data before estimating.
Add reconciliation % and error counts per run.
Business validates samples of migrated records.

types.name: Analytics / BI platform
types.plain: Building reports and dashboards so people can make decisions from data instead of spreadsheets.
types.examples: Executive dashboards, self-service BI, data warehouse

docs.note: List the decisions the dashboards will support.
Users reconcile key numbers against finance.
Track active users and decisions supported.

types.name: AI / ML pilot
types.plain: Testing whether an AI model can do a useful job (for example, predicting demand or answering customer questions) before investing more.
types.examples: GenAI assistant pilot, churn prediction, document extraction

docs.when: Light version before the pilot; full version only if the pilot succeeds.
docs.note: Define the kill criteria: what result means stop.
State the hypothesis and success threshold up front.
Include data privacy, bias and model-risk items.

docs.when: At the end of the pilot: scale, iterate or stop.
docs.note: This is the scale-up decision, not a launch.
Even a failed pilot must leave written findings.

projectCategories.name: Business Transformation
projectCategories.plain: Changing how people work: processes, structures, ways of working. Often there is no software at the centre.

types.name: Process improvement
types.plain: Making an existing way of working faster, cheaper or less error-prone, for example how invoices get approved.
types.examples: Order-to-cash redesign, Lean / Six Sigma initiative

docs.note: Include current baseline metrics for the process.

docs.when: Before and after the redesign.
docs.note: Show who does what in the new process.
Benefits are the whole point: measure them.

docs.when: Fortnightly is usually enough.

types.name: Organisational change / restructure
types.plain: Changing team structures, roles or ways of working, where helping people adapt matters more than any system.
types.examples: New operating model, merger integration, return-to-office

docs.when: Update fortnightly: sentiment shifts quickly.
docs.note: This is your most important document here.
Sequence matters: managers hear before teams.
Include people risks: attrition, morale, legal consultation.

projectCategories.name: Programs & Portfolio
projectCategories.plain: Managing several related projects together, or the whole collection of projects an organisation is running.

types.name: Multi-project program
types.plain: Several projects that together deliver one bigger goal, managed as one so their dependencies and shared resources line up.
types.examples: Digital transformation program, new market entry
types.method: Program governance over mixed project methods

docs.note: Program-level case; each project may have a short one.
Benefits usually land at program level, not project level.
Run one shared RAID log across the program.
Shared specialists are the usual bottleneck.
One view of shared specialists across all projects in the program.

types.name: PMO setup / portfolio governance
types.plain: Setting up the team and rules that oversee all projects: standard templates, reporting and how projects get approved.
types.examples: New PMO, portfolio prioritisation, governance refresh

docs.note: Becomes the PMO's main product.
Use as the base for your standard PM method.
Standardise this template across all projects.
A PMO usually owns the cross-project view of who is working where.
If the PMO also reports on utilisation.

projectCategories.name: Client Services & Agency Delivery
projectCategories.plain: Delivering work for an external client, such as a design studio or consultancy building something under contract.

types.name: Fixed-bid client engagement
types.plain: The client pays an agreed price for agreed work. Going over scope or time costs the agency money, so scope control is everything.
types.examples: Website build, app design and build, research study

docs.note: Mirror the statement of work: deliverables, assumptions, exclusions.
Map the client's real decision makers, not just your day-to-day contact.
Include client-side approvals and turnaround times.
Show client review windows as tasks with owners.

docs.when: Weekly: burn vs earned on a fixed fee.
docs.note: Track hours burned against % of deliverables accepted.
Every extra request goes through this; it protects margin.
Log client-side assumptions (content, feedback speed).
Client-facing version: no internal margin data.
Acts as the deliverable acceptance that triggers invoices.

types.name: Time & materials / retainer
types.plain: The client pays for the hours worked. The risk is less about margin and more about showing value for every hour.
types.examples: Design retainer, staff augmentation, ongoing product team

docs.note: A short engagement brief: goals, team, rate card, cap.
Doubles as the billing forecast.
Include hours used vs cap.
Helps renewals: show outcomes, not hours.

docs.when: Weekly, from timesheets.
docs.note: On T&M, billed hours are your revenue: track them against the cap.
Shows the client how much capacity they've booked ahead.

projectCategories.name: Resource Management
projectCategories.plain: Making sure the right people are on the right work at the right time, across all projects, not just one.

types.name: Staffing a new client account
types.plain: A new client or SOW has been signed and you need to put a team together quickly, with the right skills and grades.
types.examples: New logo win, new SOW on an existing account, team ramp-up

docs.when: The day the deal is likely, not the day it's signed.
docs.note: Soft-book likely people early so the start date isn't a scramble.
Match on skills and grade, not on who happens to be free.
Check the next 12 weeks, not just the start week.
Look at the bench first: placing bench people protects margin.
Use it to plan the ramp-up curve by month.
Agree who approves staffing: the account lead, delivery head or client.

types.name: Bench management and redeployment
types.plain: People are between projects. The job is to get them back onto billable work quickly, and use the gap well.
types.examples: Project ended early, campus joiners, demand slowdown

docs.when: Weekly, every Monday.
docs.note: Escalate anyone past 30 days to the delivery head.
Match open requests against the bench before approving any hiring.
Use bench time to close skill gaps the matrix shows.
Track bench % as part of overall billability.

types.name: Ramp-down and roll-off
types.plain: A project is ending or shrinking. People need to move to new work without a gap, and without losing what they know.
types.examples: Go-live and hypercare exit, contract end, scope reduction

docs.when: 6-8 weeks before the roll-off date.
docs.note: Plan the next booking before the current one ends.
Propose rolling-off people for upcoming requests first.
Anyone without a next booking goes on the tracker the day they roll off.
Capture knowledge before people move on.
Record who received each handover.

types.name: Annual capacity and hiring planning
types.plain: Working out how many people with which skills you'll need next year, and whether to hire, train or partner.
types.examples: Annual operating plan, budget cycle, new practice launch

docs.note: Forecast demand by role and month from the sales pipeline.
Supply side: what skills you have today and where they're thin.
Use the last 6-12 months as the baseline.
Lost requests show what you should have hired for.
For new hires or a new practice, show cost against expected billing.

metrics.name: Schedule Performance Index (SPI)
metrics.plain: Compares the work actually done with the work we planned to have done by now. 1.0 means exactly on plan; 0.9 means we've done 90% of what we should have.

impact.summary: The finish date is at risk. Every month below 1.0 pushes the end date further unless something changes.
effects: Downstream teams (testing, training, other projects) lose their windows
Costs rise because people stay on the project longer

diagnose: Is the slip on the critical path, or on tasks that have slack?
Is it one workstream or spread across all?
Is the cause capacity (not enough people), productivity, dependencies, or scope growth?
Was the plan realistic in the first place?
actions: Re-sequence: start non-dependent tasks in parallel (fast-tracking)
Add people to critical-path tasks only, early (crashing)
Remove blockers: escalate late dependencies
Agree a reduced scope for the first release
Re-forecast the end date honestly and raise a change request if tolerance is breached
resolution.escalate: Below 0.95 for two months running, or any milestone slip over 10 working days: take it to the Steering Committee with options.

metrics.name: Milestone variance
metrics.plain: How many working days late (or early) each key milestone is forecast to be compared with the original plan.
metrics.example: MVP build complete: baseline 26 Jun, forecast 10 Jul = +10 days

impact.summary: A late milestone usually means everything after it moves too, unless there is buffer.

diagnose: How much buffer is left before go-live?
Is the delay already absorbed by later tasks, or pushing them?
Is this the first slip or a pattern?
actions: Protect testing time: do not compress it to recover build delays
Use remaining buffer deliberately and say so
Split the milestone: deliver the critical part on time
Update all dependent teams the same day
resolution.escalate: Any slip that eats more than half of the remaining buffer, or touches a fixed external date.

metrics.name: Buffer remaining
metrics.plain: How much safety time is left between the forecast finish and the date we must hit.
metrics.example: Lighthouse: 4 weeks at baseline, 2 weeks now

impact.summary: Buffer is what lets you absorb surprises. When it's gone, every new problem becomes a missed date.
effects: No room for late defects or rework
Teams start cutting corners to hold the date

diagnose: How fast is buffer being consumed compared with project progress?
What used it up: one event or steady drift?
actions: Plan explicit buffer recovery (scope options, extra capacity)
Show buffer burn on the status report so leaders see the trend
resolution.escalate: Buffer burn faster than progress (e.g. 50% of buffer used at 30% complete).

metrics.name: Cost Performance Index (CPI)
metrics.plain: Shows how much work you're getting for each dollar spent. 1.0 means a dollar of spending buys a dollar of planned work; 0.9 means it buys only 90 cents' worth.

impact.summary: The project will cost more than budgeted. CPI rarely improves on its own after the project is 20% complete.
effects: Final cost forecast rises (EAC = Budget ÷ CPI)
For agencies on fixed price: margin disappears

diagnose: Which cost lines are over: people, vendors, licences?
Is it a one-off (e.g. a fixed problem) or a rate of overspend that will continue?
Are we earning value honestly, or claiming progress on unfinished work?
Are people charging time to the project that belongs elsewhere?
actions: Fix the root cause on the overspending workstream first
Negotiate cost sharing with the vendor where the contract allows
Reduce scope for the first release
Stop or delay non-essential spend
Raise a change request to re-baseline if the gap is permanent
resolution.escalate: Below 0.95 for two months, or forecast overrun above the PM's tolerance: change request to the sponsor / SteerCo.

metrics.name: Estimate at Completion (EAC) and Variance at Completion (VAC)
metrics.plain: EAC is today's best guess of what the project will cost in total. VAC is how far that is from the budget.
metrics.formula: EAC = Budget ÷ CPI (if overspend continues), or Actual + (Budget − Earned) (if one-off). VAC = Budget − EAC

impact.summary: Tells leaders whether to find more money now, rather than discovering it at the end.
effects: Funding requests late in the year are hard to approve
Benefits case may no longer stack up

diagnose: Which EAC formula fits: is overspend continuing or fixed?
Has the forecast been signed off by Finance?
actions: Present both EAC methods and say which you believe
Show the scope and timing options that close the gap
resolution.escalate: Any VAC beyond the remaining contingency.

metrics.name: Burn rate vs plan
metrics.plain: How fast money is being spent each month compared with the plan.
metrics.formula: Actual spend this month ÷ Planned spend this month

impact.summary: Overspending runs out of money early. Underspending can mean work is not happening, which is a schedule problem.
effects: Underspend: hidden delay, or year-end budget lost

diagnose: Is underspend caused by delayed hiring or vendor start?
Is overspend caused by more people than planned?
actions: Match spend profile to delivered work, not to the calendar
Release unused budget early if work is genuinely cheaper
resolution.escalate: Two months outside amber range in the same direction.

metricCategories.name: Scope & Requirements
metricCategories.plain: Are we building the right thing, and only that?

metrics.name: Scope change rate
metrics.plain: How much work has been added (or removed) compared with the original agreed scope.
metrics.formula: Approved change effort ÷ Original baseline effort

impact.summary: Unmanaged scope growth is the most common reason projects run late and over budget.
effects: Timeline and cost grow without a decision
Team morale drops as the finish line moves
Quality suffers as work is squeezed

diagnose: Are changes coming from one stakeholder or many?
Were requirements unclear at the start?
Are small changes being absorbed without logging?
actions: Route every change through the change request process
For each addition, ask what comes out (trade, don't add)
Hold a scope re-baselining session with the sponsor
Create a 'phase 2' list for good ideas that aren't urgent
resolution.escalate: Cumulative change above 10%, or any single change beyond the PM's authority.

metrics.name: Requirements stability / backlog churn
metrics.plain: How many requirements (or backlog items) are being changed or reworked after they were agreed.
metrics.formula: Items changed after approval ÷ Total approved items

impact.summary: High churn means the team keeps building and rebuilding; it shows the problem isn't understood yet.
effects: Velocity looks fine but outcomes don't move

diagnose: Are the right users involved early enough?
Is the Product Owner empowered to decide?
actions: Add prototyping or user testing before build
Strengthen the definition of ready
Clarify decision rights in the RACI
resolution.escalate: Churn above 20% for two sprints.

metrics.name: Scope delivered vs committed
metrics.plain: Of the features promised for a release, how many actually shipped.

impact.summary: Users and sponsors judge the project by what they receive versus what they were promised.

diagnose: Were the dropped features the low-value ones?
Was the cut decided early or forced late?
actions: Agree must-have vs nice-to-have up front (MoSCoW)
Communicate scope cuts early with the reason
resolution.escalate: Any must-have feature not delivered.

metrics.name: Open defect backlog by severity
metrics.plain: How many known bugs are still unfixed, sorted by how serious they are.
metrics.formula: Count of open defects, grouped Critical / High / Medium / Low

impact.summary: A growing bug list near launch means either a delayed go-live or a launch with known problems.
effects: Go-live delay or launch with workarounds
Users lose confidence in the new system

diagnose: Are we finding more bugs than we fix each week?
Are bugs clustered in one area or component?
Are bugs being reopened after fixes?
actions: Stop new feature work and run a bug-fix sprint
Add fix capacity to the hot-spot area
Triage daily with the Product Owner
Agree exit criteria for testing (e.g. 0 critical, ≤ 5 high)
resolution.escalate: Any critical defect open for more than 2 days, or rising backlog within 4 weeks of go-live.

metrics.name: Test pass rate
metrics.plain: Of the tests run, what percentage passed.

impact.summary: Low pass rates signal the product isn't ready; high pass rates with low coverage can be falsely reassuring.
effects: Unknown risk if coverage is low

diagnose: How many tests are blocked, not just failed?
Are failures caused by the product or by test data / environments?
actions: Fix environment and data issues first: they waste test cycles
Re-prioritise test cases around high-risk journeys
resolution.escalate: Pass rate below 85% at the planned test exit date.

metrics.name: Escaped defects
metrics.plain: Bugs found after the work was considered done, for example by users after release.
metrics.formula: Count of defects found after sprint / release completion

impact.summary: Each escaped bug costs far more to fix later and is visible to customers.

diagnose: Which test stage should have caught it?
Is there a gap in automated tests?
actions: Add a test for every escaped bug (regression)
Strengthen the definition of done
Hold a short root-cause review
resolution.escalate: Any escaped critical defect.

metrics.name: Velocity (and its stability)
metrics.plain: How much work the team completes in each sprint, measured in story points. Useful only for the team's own forecasting.
metrics.formula: Sum of story points completed in the sprint; use a 3-sprint rolling average

impact.summary: Unstable velocity makes delivery dates unreliable.
effects: Stakeholders lose trust in the team's commitments

diagnose: Were there unplanned interruptions (support, meetings, absence)?
Did team membership change?
Are stories too big to finish in one sprint?
actions: Protect the team from unplanned work (support rota)
Split stories to under 3 days each
Keep the team stable
resolution.escalate: Never use velocity to compare teams or set targets. Escalate only the forecast impact.

metrics.name: Say/do ratio (sprint commitment reliability)
metrics.plain: Of the work the team said it would finish in a sprint, how much it actually finished.

impact.summary: Consistently low say/do means planning is over-optimistic or the team keeps being interrupted.

diagnose: How much scope was added mid-sprint?
Were dependencies ready when the sprint started?
actions: Commit to the rolling-average velocity, not the hopeful number
Enforce a definition of ready
Track mid-sprint additions separately
resolution.escalate: Below 80% for two consecutive sprints.

metrics.name: Cycle time
metrics.plain: How long a piece of work takes from when someone starts it to when it's done.
metrics.formula: Done date − Start date, per item (track the 85th percentile)
metrics.example: 85% of stories finish within 6 working days

impact.summary: Long cycle times mean slow feedback and lots of half-finished work.

diagnose: Where does work wait longest (review, testing, approval)?
How much work is in progress at once?
actions: Limit work in progress
Swarm on blocked items
Remove handoff queues (e.g. embed a tester)
resolution.escalate: Rising trend for 4+ weeks.

metricCategories.name: Engineering & Release (DORA)
metricCategories.plain: How fast and safely can we release changes?

metrics.name: Deployment frequency
metrics.plain: How often the team releases changes to users (or to a test environment).

impact.summary: Infrequent releases mean big, risky launches and slow feedback.
effects: Slow reaction to bugs and feedback

diagnose: Is release manual?
Are approvals the bottleneck?
actions: Automate the build and deployment pipeline
Release smaller batches
Use feature flags to release safely
resolution.escalate: Not usually escalated; raise in tech governance.

metrics.name: Change failure rate
metrics.plain: Of all releases, what percentage caused a problem that needed fixing or rolling back.

impact.summary: High failure rates hurt users and make teams afraid to release.
effects: Slower releases as teams add manual checks

diagnose: Do failures share a cause (config, data, a component)?
Is automated test coverage adequate?
actions: Increase automated testing on risky areas
Add smoke tests after each deployment
Hold blameless post-incident reviews
resolution.escalate: Any failure causing a customer-facing outage.

metrics.name: Mean time to restore (MTTR)
metrics.plain: When something breaks, how long it takes on average to get it working again.

impact.summary: Slow recovery multiplies the impact of every failure.

diagnose: Is monitoring detecting problems quickly?
Is rollback automated?
actions: Improve alerts and dashboards
Automate rollback
Write runbooks for common failures
resolution.escalate: Any production outage longer than the agreed service level.

metricCategories.name: Risk & Governance
metricCategories.plain: Are we managing what could go wrong?

metrics.name: Open high risks
metrics.plain: How many serious risks (high probability and high impact) are currently open.
metrics.formula: Count of open risks with score ≥ 15 (probability × impact on 1-5 scales)

impact.summary: Several high risks at once mean the project could fail in more than one way.
effects: Higher chance of a major delay or overrun
Contingency may not cover what happens

diagnose: Does each high risk have an owner and a dated action?
Are mitigations actually reducing the score?
actions: Assign a single owner and a review date per risk
Fund mitigation for the top risks
Convert risks into issues as soon as they happen
resolution.escalate: Score 15+ goes to the Program Manager within 2 days; 20+ to the Steering Committee.

metrics.name: Issue ageing
metrics.plain: How long current problems have been open without being resolved.
metrics.formula: Today − Date raised, for each open issue (track the average and oldest)

impact.summary: Old issues are usually stuck waiting for a decision or another team.

diagnose: What is each old issue waiting for, and from whom?
actions: Escalate decisions needed from outside the team
Agree a due date with the owner
resolution.escalate: Any high-priority issue open more than 14 days.

metrics.name: Decision latency
metrics.plain: How long the project waits for decisions after asking for them.
metrics.example: CR-007 requested 17 Jun, decided 24 Jun = 5 working days

impact.summary: Slow decisions are one of the most common hidden causes of delay.
effects: Teams wait or build on assumptions
Rework when the decision finally comes

diagnose: Who is the decision maker, and do they know?
Was enough information provided to decide?
actions: Pre-wire decisions with options and a recommendation
Agree decision deadlines in the governance calendar
resolution.escalate: Any decision blocking critical-path work for more than 5 days.

metricCategories.name: People & Resources
metricCategories.plain: Do we have the right people, and are they OK?

metrics.name: Capacity utilisation
metrics.plain: How much of people's available time is booked onto work.
metrics.example: SI developers in June: 7 needed ÷ 6 available = 117%

impact.summary: Overloaded people burn out and make mistakes; underloaded people mean wasted cost.

diagnose: Is over-allocation in one role or across the team?
Is it temporary (a peak) or structural?
actions: Re-sequence work to flatten peaks
Bring in extra capacity for the bottleneck role
Reduce or delay scope
resolution.escalate: Any role above 100% for more than one month.

metrics.name: Team attrition / key-person risk
metrics.plain: How many people leave or rotate off the team, and whether any one person is a single point of failure.
metrics.formula: People who left in period ÷ Average team size
metrics.example: SI partner rotated 2 of 8 in May = 25%

impact.summary: Losing people mid-project loses knowledge and slows delivery while replacements ramp up.
effects: Velocity drop for 2-6 weeks per change

diagnose: Is turnover concentrated with one vendor or manager?
Who has knowledge nobody else has?
actions: Add named-resource and handover clauses with vendors
Pair people on critical knowledge
Document key designs
resolution.escalate: Loss of any single point of failure.

metrics.name: Team health / morale
metrics.plain: How the team feels: a short regular survey (e.g. 1-5 scores on workload, clarity, support).
metrics.formula: Average of anonymous pulse survey scores

impact.summary: Morale drops usually show up weeks before delivery problems do.

diagnose: Which questions dropped most?
Did something change (deadline, people, overtime)?
actions: Discuss results openly in the retrospective
Act visibly on one or two items
resolution.escalate: Sustained score below 3.0.

metricCategories.name: Stakeholders & Value
metricCategories.plain: Are people happy and are we getting the benefits?

metrics.name: Benefits realisation
metrics.plain: How much of the promised benefit (savings, revenue, satisfaction) has actually been achieved.

impact.summary: If benefits don't arrive, the investment wasn't worth it, even if the project was on time and budget.

diagnose: Are people actually using the new system or process?
Is the measurement itself reliable?
actions: Drive adoption: training, champions, remove the old way
Fix usability blockers found after launch
Re-plan the benefit timeline honestly
resolution.escalate: Any benefit forecast below 70% of target.

metrics.name: Stakeholder satisfaction
metrics.plain: How satisfied key stakeholders are with the project, from a short regular survey.
metrics.formula: Average survey score (1-5) from key stakeholders

impact.summary: Unhappy stakeholders withdraw support, block decisions or resist the change.

diagnose: Which group is least satisfied and why?
Is it about results or about communication?
actions: Meet the least satisfied stakeholders 1:1
Adjust the communication plan
Show progress they care about
resolution.escalate: Any key decision-maker scoring below 3.

metrics.name: Adoption rate
metrics.plain: Of the people who should be using the new system or process, how many actually are.

impact.summary: No adoption means no benefits. It's the bridge between delivery and value.
effects: Parallel old and new ways of working cost more

diagnose: Which teams or sites lag?
Is the old way still available?
actions: Targeted coaching for lagging teams
Switch off the old way on a set date
Collect and fix top usability complaints
resolution.escalate: Below 60% four weeks after launch.

metricCategories.name: Resource Management
metricCategories.plain: Are our people on the right work, and is it paying?

metrics.name: Billability
metrics.plain: Of the hours people were available, how many were billed to a client.
metrics.example: Brightpath, week of 15 Jun: about 76% against a 75% target

impact.summary: Low billability means you're paying for time nobody pays you for. It's the fastest way margin disappears in a services business.
effects: Margin falls even when everyone looks busy
Pricing and hiring decisions get made on false assumptions

diagnose: Is it bench, or non-billable work on live projects?
Are people doing work the SOW doesn't cover?
Are timesheets accurate?
actions: Move bench people onto open requests first
Raise change requests for unbilled scope
Cap internal work for billable roles
Fix timesheet categories so the data is trustworthy
resolution.escalate: Team billability below 65% for 4 weeks, or any account where billed effort is well below effort spent.

metrics.name: Bench % and bench ageing
metrics.plain: How many people are not on billable work, and how long they've been waiting.
metrics.formula: People on bench ÷ Total people; days since roll-off for each
metrics.example: Brightpath: 5 of 24 on bench (21%), 2 of them past 30 days

impact.summary: Bench costs money every day, and long bench stretches are when good people start interviewing elsewhere.
effects: Attrition risk among your best people

diagnose: Is bench caused by a demand drop, poor matching, or a skills mismatch?
Are bench people being proposed for open requests?
Did hiring run ahead of signed work?
actions: Propose bench people before external hires for every request
Cross-skill towards skills with open demand
Use bench time for pre-sales, internal tools or shadowing
Pause hiring for roles with people on the bench
resolution.escalate: Anyone past 30 days on bench with no next opportunity; bench above 15% for a month.

metrics.name: Time to fill
metrics.plain: How many working days it takes from a request being raised to a person being confirmed.
metrics.formula: Filled date − Raised date (working days), averaged

impact.summary: Slow fills delay project starts, and the client's first impression of a new engagement is a team that isn't there yet.
effects: Account leads go around RMG and hire or borrow on their own

diagnose: Are requests raised late, or filled slowly?
Which roles or skills take longest?
Is approval the bottleneck?
actions: Ask account leads for requests at the likely-deal stage, not after signing
Soft-book likely people early
Keep a small pool of hard-to-find skills
Agree approval turnaround times
resolution.escalate: Any request starting within 3 weeks that's still open.

metrics.name: Fill rate
metrics.plain: Of the requests that closed, how many you actually staffed.

impact.summary: Lost requests are lost revenue, and they tell clients you can't deliver what you sell.
effects: Clients go to other vendors for the work

diagnose: Which skills or grades are you losing on?
Were requests lost to timing or to skills?
actions: Hire or train for the skills you keep losing
Use partners or contractors for short spikes
Tell sales which roles you can't staff before they sell them
resolution.escalate: Two lost requests for the same skill in a quarter.

metrics.name: Allocation accuracy (planned vs actual)
metrics.plain: How closely the hours people actually logged match what they were planned to work.

impact.summary: If plans don't match reality, every capacity decision built on them is wrong.
effects: Capacity looks free when it isn't

diagnose: Are people pulled into unplanned work?
Are bookings updated when projects change?
actions: Review the heatmap weekly with PMs and update it
Log unplanned work so it becomes visible
Release bookings that won't be used
resolution.escalate: Persistent gaps on the same account or the same people.

metrics.name: Skills coverage
metrics.plain: For each skill you sell, how many people can do it without help.
metrics.formula: Count of people rated 3+ per skill
metrics.example: Brightpath: UX Design has 1 person at 3+ (Gap)

impact.summary: One person holding a skill is one resignation, illness or holiday away from a stalled project.
effects: Projects wait for one person's availability

diagnose: Which skills are thin, and which are growing in demand?
Is anyone being trained as a second?
actions: Pair a second person on thin skills
Prioritise bench time for cross-skilling
Hire for gaps that demand will grow
resolution.escalate: Any skill with demand in the pipeline and only one person able to do it.

glossary.definition: Red / Amber / Green. A traffic-light status: green is on track, amber needs attention, red needs help now.
Risks, Assumptions, Issues, Dependencies (and Decisions). The things that can derail a project, tracked in one log.
Responsible (does the work), Accountable (signs it off), Consulted (asked for input), Informed (kept updated).
Steering Committee. The group of senior leaders who make the big decisions about a project, usually monthly.
The senior leader who owns the project's purpose and budget, and who the project manager answers to.
Anyone affected by the project or able to influence it.
The approved original plan (dates, cost, scope) that progress is measured against.
A key checkpoint in the plan, such as 'design signed off' or 'go-live'. It has a date but no duration.
A chart that shows tasks as horizontal bars along a timeline.
Work Breakdown Structure. The project's work broken down into smaller, manageable pieces.
The longest chain of dependent tasks. Any delay on it delays the whole project.
A formal checkpoint where leaders decide whether the project can move to its next phase.
Earned Value Management. A way to measure progress by comparing planned work, completed work and money spent.
Planned Value. The budgeted cost of the work that should have been done by now.
Earned Value. The budgeted cost of the work actually done by now.
Actual Cost. What has actually been spent so far.
Schedule Performance Index = EV ÷ PV. Below 1.0 means behind schedule.
Cost Performance Index = EV ÷ AC. Below 1.0 means over budget.
Estimate at Completion. The forecast total cost of the project.
Budget at Completion. The total approved budget.
To-Complete Performance Index. How efficient the remaining work must be to finish on budget.
Money or time set aside for risks that might happen.
A formal request to change the agreed scope, budget or timeline. Also called a CR.
Gradual, unapproved growth in what the project is expected to deliver.
A short, fixed period (usually two weeks) in which an agile team builds and shows a working piece of the product.
How much work an agile team completes per sprint, measured in story points.
A relative measure of how much effort a piece of work needs. Used by agile teams instead of hours.
A chart showing how much work is left in a sprint, day by day. It should slope down to zero.
The prioritised list of work still to be done.
The person who decides what the team builds and in what order.
The person who helps an agile team work well and removes blockers.
User Acceptance Testing. Real users test the system to confirm it does what the business needs.
System Integration Testing. Checking that connected systems work together correctly.
The moment the new system or process starts being used for real.
The planned switch from the old system to the new one, usually over a weekend.
Undoing a launch and returning to the old system if something goes wrong.
Extra-intensive support for the first weeks after go-live.
Four measures of software delivery performance from Google's DevOps Research and Assessment team.
Mean Time To Restore. How long it takes, on average, to fix something that broke.
Full-Time Equivalent. 1 FTE = one person working full time; 0.5 FTE = half their time.
Subject Matter Expert. Someone who knows a business area or system in depth.
Statement of Work. The contract document describing what a supplier will deliver.
Net Present Value. Today's value of future gains minus costs. Positive means worth doing.
Internal Rate of Return. The yearly return the investment earns, as a percentage.
How long until the money gained equals the money spent.
Project Management Office. The team that sets standards and oversees projects.
Proving that the project delivered the value it promised, after it finishes.
The agreed checklist a piece of work must meet before it counts as finished.
A contract where the client pays an agreed price for agreed work, whatever the effort.
A contract where the client pays for the hours actually worked.
A way to prioritise: Must have, Should have, Could have, Won't have this time.
People who are not currently on billable client work, usually between projects.
The share of someone's available hours that was billed to a client.
The share of someone's available hours spent on project work, billable or not.
Resource Management Group. The team that assigns people to projects across an organisation.
A provisional reservation of a person for a likely project, before the contract is signed.
A confirmed assignment of a person to a project.
How long it takes to staff a role after the request is raised.
Adding people to a project as work grows.
Moving people off a project as work shrinks or ends. Also called roll-off.
A grid of people against skills, showing how strong each person is at each skill.
The list of upcoming requests for people, from likely deals to signed work.
